newsitem.title: UK: Major tabloid deserts Britain's Conservatives.
newsitem.headline: Major tabloid deserts Britain's Conservatives.

text.p: Britain's best-selling Sunday tabloid newspaper said it was deserting the ruling Conservative Party and backing the opposition Labour party, clear favourite to win the May 1 national election.

But the influential Sunday Times said it was staying with Prime Minister John Major's party, saying that what it described as Labour's "safe sex" option -- "all the fun and no risk" -- was not as secure as it seemed.

The News of the World was the second big newspaper to change sides and thrown its weight behind Tony Blair's revamped Labour Party, reflecting a widespread sentiment that it was time for a change after 18 years of Conservative rule.
Its top-selling sister daily The Sun, owned by Australian-born media magnate Ruper Murdoch, did the same last month.
"We back Blair, the man for the new millenium," the News of the World, which sells around 4.5 million copies a week, declared in a front-page story for its Sunday edition.
"Britain is crying out for strong and moral leadership. John Major has provided neither," it added.

The Sunday Times, also owned by Murdoch, said the Conservative record over the past five years was "dismal". But it questioned whether newly-reformed Labour could be trusted and said the party was at odds over privatisation.
"Why ape those very Tory policies that Labour has consistently opposed? Put bluntly, why not vote Tory if you want Tory policies?" it asked.
On the final weekend of campaigning, opinion polls showed Labour maintaining the double-digit lead it has held in every poll bar one for the past five weeks.
A poll for the Sunday Mirror newspaper gave Labour a hefty 24-points ahead, which would give the party a landslide victory unseen since 1945.

Major said the vibrant economy his party had created would disappear if Labour took power, claiming his opponents would raise public spending, introduce a national minimum wage and give trade unions greater powers.
Labour hammered away at what it sees as a key weakness of the Conservatives -- voters' fears that it could put tax on food and other essentials.
The two parties united only on their determination not to allow the Irish Republican Army to disrupt Thursday's poll.
Following a spate of bombs and bomb scares on the British mainland, the government has sent election officials instructions on how to deal with bomb threats.
